# In Praise of Almost

"Almost" may be the most hopeful word in English, and also the most sorrowful.

Consider what it does. It stands at the edge of a fact and refuses to step over. *Almost home. Almost finished. Almost said it.* Each phrase holds two worlds at once: the one that happened, and the one that hovered close enough to touch. Most words commit to a single reality. "Almost" keeps the door ajar on the other one.

I think we underestimate how much of life happens in that gap. The kettle almost boiling has a particular sound, a low rising murmur that isn't quite the roar yet. Anyone who has stood in a kitchen at six in the morning knows it. The moment before a sneeze, before a laugh, before someone walks into a room. The gray light that is almost morning. These aren't lesser versions of the completed thing. They have their own texture, often more vivid than the event itself, because possibility is still humming in them and nothing has yet been decided.

The sad side is real, of course. Almost is the word of near-misses, of the email drafted and never sent, of the bridge that stopped a few feet short of the far bank. Regret loves that word. It's easier to mourn a thing that nearly happened than one that was never possible, because the nearly-happened thing comes with a blueprint. You can see exactly where the wall was thin.

But I've come to think the two sides of the word are really one. Both come from the same fact: the world is less settled than it looks. Whatever is, was once almost something else. Every finished thing, the bridge and the friendship and the poem, passed through a long season of almost, and might not have made it. That's a little frightening, but it's also generous. It means the unfinished things in our lives aren't failures in waiting. They're just in the stretch of the story where the kettle is murmuring, and the light is gray, and something is about to arrive.

So here's to the almosts: the drafts, the half-built things, the sentences that trail off and could still go anywhere.

This one, though, I'll let finish.
